content: The document outlines a generic protocol for developing and maintaining systematic reviews that evaluate interventions for treating pre-eclampsia and its complications. This protocol provides a standardized methodology for selecting and assessing studies, developed in consultation with existing review authors. The aim is to ensure a systematic and comprehensive approach to the topic, increasing consistency across reviews, and making them easier to read and use. Any significant deviations from this protocol in individual reviews will be explicitly stated. Hypertension, or high blood pressure, is a common condition during pregnancy, affecting approximately 10% of women at some point before delivery. Pre-eclampsia, also known as toxemia, is defined as hypertension accompanied by proteinuria (protein in the urine). It typically occurs in the second half of pregnancy and complicates 2% to 8% of pregnancies. While women with hypertension alone generally have pregnancy outcomes similar to those with normal blood pressure, outcomes worsen significantly when proteinuria develops. Many women with pre-eclampsia are asymptomatic, but severe cases or very high blood pressure can cause symptoms such as headaches, upper abdominal pain, or visual disturbances. Pre-eclampsia can lead to complications in the liver, kidneys, brain, and clotting system. Rare but serious complications include eclampsia (seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia), stroke, HELLP syndrome (hemolysis, elevated liver enzymes, and low platelets), and disseminated intravascular coagulation. These complications are associated with an increased risk of maternal death. Pre-eclampsia can also affect the placenta, increasing risks for the baby, including poor intrauterine growth and premature birth. Although most women recover well after pre-eclampsia or eclampsia, these conditions remain significant causes of maternal mortality. Over half a million women die annually from pregnancy-related causes, with 99% of these deaths occurring in developing countries. Maternal mortality rates in low-income countries are 100 to 200 times higher than in Europe and North America. Women in industrialized countries have a lifetime risk of dying from pregnancy-related causes of 1 in 4,000 to 1 in 10,000, compared to 1 in 15 to 1 in 50 in low-income countries. Pre-eclampsia accounts for an estimated 10% to 15% of maternal deaths in developing countries and 13% to 15% of direct obstetric deaths in the UK and USA. Perinatal mortality is also increased following pre-eclampsia, and morbidity for both mother and baby is likely high. For example, pre-eclampsia accounts for one-fifth of antenatal admissions and two-thirds of referrals to day care assessment units in the UK, as well as a quarter of obstetric admissions to intensive care units in France. The underlying cause of pre-eclampsia remains unclear, and the only definitive treatment is delivery of the baby. Interventions aim to treat symptoms, prevent complications, and optimize the timing of delivery. Pre-eclampsia is part of a spectrum of hypertensive disorders of pregnancy, which range from normal pregnancy to severe disease. During normal pregnancy, significant maternal physiological adaptations occur, including increased cardiac output and changes in blood pressure. In contrast, pre-eclampsia involves widespread endothelial dysfunction, vasoconstriction, and activation of the coagulation system, leading to clinical manifestations such as hypertension, proteinuria, and organ dysfunction. Hypertension in pregnancy is defined as a systolic blood pressure of at least 140 mmHg, a diastolic blood pressure of at least 90 mmHg, or both. Proteinuria is defined as 300 mg or more of protein in a 24-hour urine sample. Severe pre-eclampsia is characterized by features such as severe hypertension, significant proteinuria, reduced urinary output, neurological disturbances, upper abdominal pain, pulmonary edema, impaired liver function, high serum creatinine, low platelets, and intrauterine growth restriction. Eclampsia, the occurrence of seizures in a woman with pre-eclampsia, is rare but serious. Magnesium sulfate is the anticonvulsant of choice for treating eclampsia, significantly reducing the risk of further seizures compared to other agents. Despite advances in understanding the pathophysiology of pre-eclampsia, its underlying cause remains unclear. Factors such as maternal age, parity, obesity, immune response, genetic predisposition, and vascular disease may play a role. Pre-eclampsia is thought to result from inadequate blood supply to the placenta, leading to the release of factors that cause endothelial dysfunction. Screening for women at risk of pre-eclampsia is an essential part of antenatal care, but no diagnostic tests have proven to be of good predictive value. Current prevention strategies include antenatal surveillance, lifestyle modification, nutritional supplementation, and pharmacological therapy. Magnesium sulfate is now the standard for preventing eclampsia, and its use has significantly reduced the incidence of eclampsia in developed countries. However, in developing countries, eclampsia remains more common and accounts for a significant proportion of maternal deaths. The management of pre-eclampsia involves monitoring and controlling blood pressure, detecting and treating complications, and optimizing the timing of delivery. Antihypertensive drugs are mandatory for severe hypertension, with the goal of achieving a smooth reduction in blood pressure to safe levels for both mother and fetus. Delivery remains the only definitive cure for pre-eclampsia, and decisions about timing depend on balancing maternal and fetal risks. For women with severe pre-eclampsia before 32 to 34 weeks of gestation, the timing of delivery is a major dilemma, requiring careful consideration of maternal and fetal needs. This generic protocol serves as a template for updating existing reviews and conducting new ones relevant to the treatment of women with pre-eclampsia. It aims to provide a systematic and comprehensive approach to the topic, ensuring consistency and clarity across reviews.
